Each arc picks its target with weight alpha plus the target's current in-degree, so a smaller alpha concentrates arcs on a few popular nodes: the most popular node receives 5, 6, and 7 arcs. Repeated arcs and opposite arcs are drawn bowed apart; self-loops are turned off." width="100%"} Repeatedly picks, uniformly at random, a node that has fewer than `k` out-edges and gives it a new out-edge to a node chosen with probability proportional to `alpha` plus that node's current in-degree. This continues until every node has `k` out-edges, so there are `n * k` edges. A large `alpha` makes the targets nearly uniform, while a small one lets the rich get richer and gives a heavy-tailed in-degree distribution. Parallel edges can appear, and so can self-loops unless `self_loops=False`. The model is due to Peterson and Pittel; the process follows NetworkX's `random_k_out_graph()`. In an undirected graph the same edges are added without their direction. The graph is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Random k-out graphs are useful for: - modeling networks where everyone makes the same number of choices, e.g. nominations, follows, or votes, but popularity varies - tuning in-degree inequality through `alpha=` while out-degrees stay fixed - random directed graphs with a fixed out-degree, e.g. for random walks ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes. [k]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Out-degree of every node. [alpha]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Initial attractiveness of every node. Must be positive. Smaller values give a more unequal in-degree distribution. [self_loops]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), a node may pick itself as a target. If `False`, it never does. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Integer seed for the random number generator. The same `seed=` with the same other arguments always gives the same graph. If `None` (default), the graph differs on every call. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each new node is labelled with its node ID as a string; a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added. If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `n=` or `k=` is negative, `alpha=` is not positive, or `self_loops=False` with a single node and `k=` above `0`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Every node has the same out-degree: ::: {#d8882d08 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_random_k_out_graph( n=100, k=3, alpha=0.5, self_loops=False, seed=4 ) graph.count_edges(), {graph.get_out_degree(v) for v in graph.get_node_ids()} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (300, {3}) ``` ::: ::: A smaller `alpha=` lets the most popular node attract more of the edges: ::: {#befc645b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} [ max( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_random_k_out_graph(n=100, k=3, alpha=alpha, seed=4) .get_in_degree(v) for v in range(1, 101) ) for alpha in (10.0, 1.0, 0.1) ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [10, 16, 34] ``` ::: :::
